slides.text:
Observed behavior : The base version of a conflicted file (git show :1:path, or the middle
                    section in diff3 style) contains conflict markers labelled
                    "Temporary merge branch 1" and "Temporary merge branch 2".
Git state         : git merge-base --all prints two commits; neither is an ancestor of the other.
Mechanism         : The ort strategy first merges the two merge bases with each other. That inner
                    merge conflicts, and its result, markers included, becomes the base.
Root cause        : A criss-cross. Each branch merged the other, and the two merges resolved the
                    same conflict in opposite ways.
Why Git does this : Either base alone would silently reapply one side's old decision, as the
                    two-answer transcript shows. A base that matches neither tip returns the
                    question to a human.
Correct fix       : Resolve it as an ordinary conflict. Read the inner block as the two earlier
                    decisions and the outer sides as the two current values.
Prevention        : Between long-lived branches, merge in one direction only. Keep other
                    branches short enough that they never merge each other.

items: Expecting Git to "replay" the branch's commits. Root cause: a merge is computed from three snapshots; the commits between the base and each tip do not take part.
A reverted change comes back after a merge. Root cause: the side that made and undid the change counts as having done nothing, and the other side still has the change.
Not noticing that both sides made the same change. Root cause: identical changes are taken once and silently; the merge prints no message for that row.
The base version of a conflicted file contains conflict markers. Root cause: a criss-cross history with two merge bases; ort merged them into a virtual base, markers included.
Trusting git merge-base without --all in a tangled history. Root cause: it prints one merge base, and which best one is output is unspecified.

beats.text: A release manager reports: "The same conflict keeps coming back." Every time main and the release branch are merged, the judge temperature in the evaluation configuration conflicts. They resolve it. Next week it conflicts again. And when they open the base version of the file, to see what both sides started from, the base version itself contains conflict markers. How can a starting point contain a conflict? Take a guess, out loud.

beats.text: Nothing is corrupt. The two branches have each merged the other, and they resolved the same conflict in opposite ways. The history now has two equally good common ancestors, and Git has to reconcile those first. To follow that, you need the rule by which every true merge is computed: three inputs, one table, and nothing else. Keep those markers inside the base in mind. You'll see them on screen.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A commit is one saved snapshot of your project, a branch is a name for a line of commits, and a merge combines two branches. In the last video, a merge either moved a ref or reported that there was nothing to do. Now both sides have commits that the other lacks, and Git has to produce a new snapshot.

beats.text: The true merge. In one sentence: when both sides have commits that the other lacks, Git combines the two tips against their merge base, path by path and then line by line, and records the result as a commit with two parents. The merge base, from the last video, is the most recent commit that both histories contain.

The merge base, from the last video, is the most recent commit that both histories contain.

beats.text: Three trees. Call them base, ours and theirs. A tree here is the full snapshot of files that one commit records. Ours is the commit HEAD points to, the branch you're on. Theirs is the commit named on the command line. For every path, Git compares three blob IDs. A blob is one file's content, and its ID is computed from that content.

beats.text: Two consequences. First, most paths are settled without reading a file. Identical content has the identical blob ID, as video 7 showed, and different content has a different one. So comparing three IDs is enough.
beats.tele: Two consequences. First, most paths are settled without reading a file. Identical content has the identical blob ID, as video 7 showed, and different content has a different one. So comparing three IDs is enough.

beats.text: Second, the rows mention three snapshots and nothing else. The commits between the base and each tip don't take part. A change that both sides made is taken once, and silently. And a change that one side made and later undid counts as "that side did nothing".
beats.tele: Second, the rows mention three snapshots and nothing else. The commits between the base and each tip don't take part. A change that both sides made is taken once, and silently. And a change that one side made and later undid counts as "that side did nothing".

beats.text: Quick quiz on that last sentence. Both branches contain a change. One branch then reverts it, with a new commit that undoes it. After the merge, is the change A, gone, or B, back? Your answer?

beats.text: B. It comes back, and this is objective three, so follow it to the end. At merge time, the tip of the branch that reverted equals the base for those lines: row "X, X, Y" or "X, Y, X". The other side changed it, and this side "did nothing". The result takes the change. The revert has no vote, because the merge never looks at the commits in between. Almost everyone is surprised by this once.

beats.text: Inside .git. A clean true merge writes a blob for every file merged by content, the trees above those blobs, and one commit object with two parent lines. Then it does what any commit does: the current branch ref moves to the new commit, and the reflogs gain a line. ORIG_HEAD holds the previous tip. git merge is 🟡 CAUTION.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. A clean true merge writes a blob for every file merged by content, the trees above those blobs, and one commit object with two `parent` lines. Then it does what any commit does: the current branch ref moves to the new commit, and the reflogs gain a line. `ORIG_HEAD` holds the previous tip. `git merge` is 🟡 CAUTION.

beats.text: Criss-cross histories. In one sentence: when two branches have each merged the other, they can have two best common ancestors, and Git then merges those ancestors with each other first, and uses the result as the base.
beats.tele: Criss-cross histories. In one sentence: when two branches have each merged the other, they can have two best common ancestors, and Git then merges those ancestors with each other first, and uses the result as the base.

beats.text: Precisely. git merge-base --all prints every merge base. Without --all you get one, and the manual says "it is unspecified which best one is output". The default strategy, named ort, handles the case as the manual describes: "When there is more than one common ancestor that can be used for 3-way merge, it creates a merged tree of the common ancestors and uses that as the reference tree for the 3-way merge". That merged tree is called the virtual merge base.
beats.tele: Precisely. `git merge-base --all` prints every merge base. Without `--all` you get one, and the manual says "it is unspecified which best one is output". The default strategy, named `ort`, handles the case as the manual describes: "When there is more than one common ancestor that can be used for 3-way merge, it creates a merged tree of the common ancestors and uses that as the reference tree for the 3-way merge". That merged tree is called the virtual merge base.

beats.text: Inside .git: the virtual merge base is computed during the merge and never becomes a commit. Its only visible trace is stage 1 of a conflicted path.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: the editor-in-chief has three copies on the desk: Monday's, yours and theirs. If only one of you changed a page, take that version. If both made the same change, take it once. If both changed it differently, open the page and compare paragraphs.

beats.text: The analogy breaks where it matters most: the editor-in-chief reads for meaning. Git compares text.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks where it matters most: the editor-in-chief reads for meaning. Git compares text.

beats.text: For the criss-cross: two Monday copies, each containing a decision that one editor made and the other rejected. Before the editor-in-chief can compare Friday's copies, the two Monday copies have to be reconciled into one. The analogy breaks when they can't be: Git then keeps the disagreement inside the base, as conflict markers.

beats.text: The script aborts the merge and repeats it with the diff3 conflict style, which shows the nesting in one view. git merge --abort is 🔴 DANGEROUS, so the five questions. What it changes: it resets the index and the working tree to HEAD, and deletes the merge state. What it can destroy: every resolution made so far, and any uncommitted edit that was staged during the merge.

beats.text: How to preview: git status and git diff --cached --stat. How to recover: staged content survives as unreferenced objects that git fsck lists, and unstaged resolution edits are gone. When it is appropriate: when the merge was a mistake or needs a different approach, as here, where nothing has been resolved yet.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Expecting Git to "replay" the branch's commits. Root cause: a merge is computed from three snapshots; the commits between the base and each tip do not take part.
beats.tele: Expecting Git to "replay" the branch's commits. Root cause: a merge is computed from three snapshots; the commits between the base and each tip do not take part.

beats.text: A reverted change comes back after a merge. Root cause: the side that made and undid the change counts as having done nothing, and the other side still has the change.
beats.tele: A reverted change comes back after a merge. Root cause: the side that made and undid the change counts as having done nothing, and the other side still has the change.

beats.text: Not noticing that both sides made the same change. Root cause: identical changes are taken once and silently; the merge prints no message for that row.
beats.tele: Not noticing that both sides made the same change. Root cause: identical changes are taken once and silently; the merge prints no message for that row.

beats.text: The base version of a conflicted file contains conflict markers. Root cause: a criss-cross history with two merge bases; ort merged them into a virtual base, markers included.
beats.tele: The base version of a conflicted file contains conflict markers. Root cause: a criss-cross history with two merge bases; `ort` merged them into a virtual base, markers included.

beats.text: Trusting git merge-base without --all in a tangled history. Root cause: it prints one merge base, and which best one is output is unspecified.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The usual producers of a criss-cross, according to the textbook, are a release branch and main that merge each other "to stay in sync", and two developers who each pull the other's feature branch. The reported symptom is "the same conflict keeps coming back". So run git merge-base --all before theorizing.

beats.text: And a consequence of the true merge for every team with CI, the automated tests that run on each change. The tree of a merge commit is a snapshot that neither author wrote, and that no test has run on. Both parents can be green while the merge is red, so CI has to run on the merge result.
